comments.value:
Changing fog is a Very Bad Idea, and to explain why I need to break down how fog works.
In Unity, fog is a scene-wide setting. There are 3 types of fog in Unity: Linear, Exponential, and Exponential Squared, with very different falloffs. There is also None, or no fog. When activated, it sets the appropriate keyword for the type of fog being used. It also provides the materials with the distance parameters and colour of the fog.
So, why is this suggestion bad? 
First, you can't have multiple types of fog active at once. If you enable linear fog, you'll override any exponential fog the scene has set. This can obviously break the visuals of a scene. 
Okay, fine. It's easy to use fog for game mechanics and stuff too but I guess we can just rule that out if this is implemented. But there's more.
Second, a scene won't necessarily have a fog colour set up. Fog in Unity always fades to a flat colour. By default, that colour is either white or black. Also, this colour can't be edited as a HDR value without an editor script. Basically, unless the scene is already designed with fog in mind, the transition will be harsh and ugly. The fog colour has no relation to the skybox colour or setting in Unity, so **it won't look smooth**.
Okay, fine. We can accept some visual sacrifice for utility, right?
Third, a scene won't necessarily have shaders included for other fog types. To reiterate, fog is a setting that is applied to the materials in the scene. That means the shaders on those materials have to support fog. For larger shaders, like even just Unity Standard, adding fog support increases the number of shaders included in the bundle exponentially. So Unity defaults to stripping unused shader variants when building bundles of a scene, *including unused variants of fog.* It's possible for the SDK to disable this setting, but this increase the size of scene and there are commonly used tools to deep-clean shaders before they're uploaded to really remove all unused or unuseable variants. So **it won't work in many circumstances**.
So, that's bad right?
Also, fog is useful for providing extra information to scene shaders. In SDK2 maps I used fog to provide extra data to some shaders. This is a niche usage but that will also break with this change. On the other hand it's easy to make a custom shader without fog support or broken fog support. Those could react in bad ways when fog is forced on. 
Finally, while I don't think adjusting the far clip plane for this feature is the worst idea, it better come with a big red warning sign and a confirmation dialogue and everything, because it's pretty typical to set up the skybox for a scene and visual effects inside it as some gigantic mesh scaled to cover the scene or player's viewport, and those will break with the far clip plane is changed. For example, I released a prefab which adds sun shafts to the world when looking at the sun. However, to make this easy, I put this on a big mesh you can cover your scene in. If the far extents of that mesh are clipped, you'll see holes in the layer of sun shafts covering your screen. That's pretty bad.

@{5d21c1a8154b187933d51a3e|full_name}:
1. As it stands **adjusting near-clip already breaks the visuals in the scene**. The purpose of fog is **to reduce the extent at which this is noticeable.**
2. You are wrong about changing the fog color; VRChat developers **are not limited to the same constraints as world developers.** [RenderSettings.fogColor](https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/RenderSettings-fogColor.html) is part of the core modules, not an Editor function, as is other functions to progmatically adjust fog.
3. VRChat devs could infer a color to use for the fog when initializing the scene. It's not rocket science, here.
4. **This is the only place where you are entirely correct;** *It would appear that since Unity 5, fog support is compiled in on build rather than patched at runtime. VRChat would either have to implement their own form of patching system, or risk the fog being non-functional in some worlds.* — **For this reason alone fog may not be possible.**
5. **I reiterate: visuals are already breaking with near-clip adjustments. This feedback is a suggestion on how to improve said visuals, smooth out certain errors.**
In all, you seem to have completely missed the point of my feedback. It's not for performance; it's to make near-clip adjustment look less broken, and reduce floating point errors caused by high far-clip. Worlds are already being broken without it.
**The suggestion is also to make it optional.** It needs no more a warning than near-clip adjustments themselves do.
@{5a9b3ad0f5e0532e3ea468be|full_name}: You're misinterpreting what I wrote. Please read it again for good measure.

@{5d21c1a8154b187933d51a3e|full_name}: What you wrote sounds like you're saying what i requested is bad for world creators, and therefore shouldn't exist.
I don't gloss over things; i wouldn't have itemized my response otherwise.
You do make a valid point about shaders needing fog support, however the majority of your post doesn't seem to focus on this.
My entire point was that near-clip is *already* breaking worlds, so if the feature is to exist, optional adjustments to *smooth* visual errors would be a decent way to go about it.
Like, your opinion is valid, from a world creator's stand point. But at the same time there's more than just world creators on VRChat.
Are there technical hurdles? Yes. Is it *possible* it's a bad idea? Yes.
But you straight up said "No it's bad" and only one or two reasons you listed are technically problematic.

author.name: Scout - VRChat Head of Quality Assurance

details:
As a potential resolution/mitigation to visual errors introduced by custom Near-Clip in worlds with large Far-Clip distances, I suggest the following:
- When custom Near-Clip is enabled, display a checkbox to "Dynamically Adjust Far-Clip"
- When Dynamic Far-Clip is **enabled**, Far-Clip amounts over 1000m will be clamped by a factor *similar to Dynamic Near-Clip*. This will attempt to keep a larger far-clip, whilst balancing it with the reduced Near-Clip.
- **Additionally**, in worlds with Far-Clip amounts over 1000m, Linear Fog will be applied at the edge of the Far-Clip distance, by about 10% the total Far-Clip. (**e.g. a Far-Clip of 10000m would produce linear fog starting at 9000m, with full coverage ending at 10000m.**) This would effectively "smooth" visual clipping and prevent "pop-in" for users with a custom Near-Clip set.
title: [1220] Add the option for Dynamic Far-Clip + Fog
